doc.title: Earl May interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2001

title: China Boy record, the violin, and the dream of jazz
summary: As a small child staying with relatives, May hears 'China Boy' on a victrola, wants guitar, is given violin, and dreams of playing in a jazz band.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: What led you into thinking that music could be a career. Because I know that you didn’t quite start out as a musician, did you?

I’ve always had a thought about playing music. Always. Even when I was a little kid. Because this is sort of personal, but my mother and father really didn’t get along too well. So I was probably — it’s not probably, I did — I stayed with every relative, aunt and uncle and cousin and you know like that, that was in this neighborhood. So I was staying with my aunt, and my cousin who was going to school at that time — we’re talking about when I was three or four years old — I would be in the house by myself. I’m going crazy and driving her nuts. She would send me down to the basement. There was an old victrola, a wind-up, and it was, “Go down there and play any records.” So I fell in over this tune, a record, I never knew who it was, but it was “China Boy” [scats]. And I wanted to play the guitar, because that was the predominant instrument on that record.

And when my mother came out to visit and she told me that my cousin, who was two years older than I was, is going to study the piano and she wanted to know what instrument I wanted to play, I said I don’t know what it’s called but I knew it had strings. You know, I’m thinking about the guitar. She gives me the violin. So I wound up studying the violin until I was about nine years old. And I hated it. But I’ve always had dreams from that record, of going in the basement, I’ve always had dreams of being on the stage and playing in a jazz band. That’s what I always wanted to do, ever since I was a little kid.
Who do you suppose that was? Like Eddie Condon?
Oh I have no idea who that was. I have not a clue.
A lot of people did that tune I know.
So it could have been any number—

It’s hard to say, and even if I heard it now I don’t know if I would, you know. But my mother says that when she was carrying me she would go up to the Apollo once a week, so she thinks that’s where it all started. I don’t know whether that’s true or not but it could be.
It makes for a good story. You were absorbing it. But you found the bass eventually.
